column6: Both paragraphs convey the same theological message about the inevitability of facing the consequences of sin and the impossibility of escaping God's judgment after death, despite any perceived avoidance of punishment in life.
column7: We will likely face the consequence of sin in our natural lives. We may perhaps feel that we’ve somehow escaped from some portion of the punishment, but there will be no escape man can make on his own accord against God’s judgment after our natural death.
column8: We are very likely to face the consequences of sin in this life. We may think we have somehow escaped certain punishments, but after death, when facing God's judgment, there is absolutely no way for a person to escape on his own.

column6: Both paragraphs convey the same core idea that the books of the Bible address sin in different ways, specifically highlighting the legal aspects of the Torah as it relates to sin and punishment. The terminology and phrasing have been altered, but the overall meaning remains consistent.
column7: The books of the Bible focus on the issue of sin differently. When Moses recorded the law in the Torah (the first five books of the Old Testament) he recorded specific punishments for specific sins/crimes. I use the word crime here interchangeably, because the books of the law were the legal system of the day for the Israelites.
column8: The various books of the Bible place different emphases on the issue of sin. When Moses recorded the Law in the Torah (the first five books of the Old Testament), he prescribed specific penalties for particular sins/offenses. Here I use “offense” and “sin” interchangeably, because the Law functioned as the legal system of Israel at the time.

column7: The reality is we are all guilty of sin, and we must all pay the price for our transgression.
